pedagogy.summary: At 8-9 the reasoning practice turns outward: children stop merely explaining their own method and begin CRITIQUING someone else's, and they string more than one fact into a chain ('since 6×10=60 and 6×2=12, then 6×8=60−12=48'). Two moves define the level — building a multi-step argument, and diagnosing why a peer's method fails, not just that its answer is wrong. This is the SMP3 'construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others' pairing made age-appropriate: arguments still lean on concrete referents (fraction bars, place-value equipment) but now demand a because/therefore link between steps. It is best taught not as a solo skill but through structured talk — analysing a deliberately flawed worked example, agreeing whether an argument 'makes sense', and being asked 'which STEP is wrong and why?' rather than 'is the answer right?'
bestPractices: Give children a peer's WRONG-but-plausible worked example (e.g. a column subtraction where the exchange was mis-recorded) and ask them to locate the faulty STEP and say why it breaks — not to redo it and compare answers
Model and require because/therefore connectives so a chain of facts becomes an argument ('since… and… therefore…'), scribing the child's spoken chain when their reasoning outruns their writing
Use 'convince me / convince a doubter' talk routines so an assertion is pushed into a justification; treat 'it just is' as the start, not the end
Anchor arguments in a shared representation (fraction bar, base-ten blocks) both parties can point at, so a critique targets the reasoning and not the person
Teach that finding one clear error and explaining it is worth more than re-solving — error analysis is the practice, per SMP3's 'distinguish correct logic from flawed logic and explain the flaw'
keyRepresentations: Fraction bars / area models for size arguments (more equal parts ⇒ smaller pieces, so 1/3 > 1/5)
Place-value equipment or a written column layout for locating an exchange error
A because/therefore sentence frame turning a list of facts into a chain
Derived-fact number strings (6×10, 6×2 ⇒ 6×8) shown as a linked sequence, not isolated facts
commonMisconceptions: 'It's wrong because the answer's different from mine' — judges a peer's argument by answer-agreement rather than by finding the flawed step
Checking one example and treating the rule as proved for all cases
Restating the method louder instead of giving a reason why it works
Believing a longer fraction/denominator names a bigger piece (1/5 > 1/3)

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, reasoning turns outward: children stop merely explaining their own method and begin critiquing someone else's, and they chain multiple facts into a single argument ('since 6×10=60 and 6×2=12, then 6×8=60−12=48'). Two moves define this level — building a multi-step because/therefore argument, and diagnosing WHY a peer's method fails (which step broke, not just that the answer differs). Arguments still lean on concrete referents (fraction bars, place-value equipment) but now require a because/therefore link between steps. Best taught through structured talk — analysing a deliberately flawed worked example, agreeing whether an argument 'makes sense', and asking 'which STEP is wrong and why?' rather than 'is the answer right?'

activities.title: Convince-me dialogue: catch the broken step
feedback: Name whether the faulty step was correctly located, not whether an answer matches: 'Yes — that flip is the broken line. Now tell me why flipping isn't allowed.'
If the child only announces the right answer ('it's 25'), redirect: 'Don't tell me the right answer yet — show me the first line where their thinking stops being okay, and say why that line breaks.'

If the child senses the error but cannot articulate it, revoice/scribe: offer 'you can't do that because…?' and let the child complete it; point at base-ten equipment so the reason has something to attach to. The reasoning is present even when the telling lags — do not treat this as not-knowing.

If the child agrees you can 'just do 6 take 1' because 'you always take the little one from the big one', this is a genuine false belief about the algorithm: build 71 with base-ten equipment, try to remove 6 ones, and force the exchange before returning to the argument skill.
activities.rationale: The level's core — constructing a chain and critiquing another's — is intrinsically dialogic. An in-role partner that asserts a flawed argument and asks the child to find and explain the broken step exercises SMP3's critique half, and 'how do you know?' pressure pushes the child's own assertions into because-clauses in real time. Children's reasoning frequently runs ahead of their ability to communicate it, so eliciting and scribing is appropriate rather than judging by fluency.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others; elementary students construct arguments using concrete referents; they distinguish correct logic from flawed, and if there is a flaw, explain what it is; all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions.

Reasoning develops along a describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder, and children's reasoning frequently runs ahead of their ability to communicate it, so a teacher must elicit and scribe the reasoning rather than judge it by fluency of telling.
learnerActions: Listen to or read a plausible-but-wrong worked chain, e.g. a partner says: 'I did 71 minus 46. I couldn't do 1 take 6, so I did 6 take 1, that's 5, then 7 take 4 is 3, so 35.'
Point to the EXACT line where the thinking first goes wrong (the digit-flip), rather than re-solving and comparing totals.
Say WHY that line breaks, grounded in place value: 'you can't flip the digits; the 1 is really part of 71, so you exchange a ten to make 11, and 11 take 6 is 5.'
When challenged with 'how do you know?' or 'why does exchanging fix it?', keep going until the objection becomes a because-chain.
Then construct a correct chain aloud for 71 − 46, starting from what 71 really is (giving 25).
activities.intendedInsight: Critiquing someone else's error forces your own reasoning to become explicit: a vague 'that's not right' can be turned, under questioning, into a because-chain you did not know you had.

activities.title: Build-an-argument workspace: chain the facts, mark the flaw
feedback: Report whether the flaw was correctly located, not whether a final answer matches.
If the child's chain lists facts without connectives, prompt: 'What word joins these two so the second follows from the first?'
If the marked step is wrong, ask the child to read each line aloud and test whether it genuinely follows from the one before.
activities.rationale: A build-an-argument workspace lets the child assemble a chain and mark the exact faulty step, making the 'which step, and why' move concrete and productive. Dragging/snapping tiles and tapping the broken step are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not required. This complements rather than replaces talk.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others; elementary students construct arguments using concrete referents; they distinguish correct logic from flawed, and if there is a flaw, explain what it is; all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions.
learnerActions: Assemble fact tiles ('6×10=60', '6×2=12') into a because/therefore sequence and write the linking reason, e.g. 'since 6×10=60 and 6×2=12, then 6×8=60−12=48.'
In a separate flawed worked example (a column subtraction with a mis-recorded exchange), tap or mark the single broken step and write or pick why it fails.
Check your own chain reads as 'since… and… therefore…', not just a list of true facts side by side.
activities.intendedInsight: A string of true facts only becomes an argument when because/therefore links them; locating 'which step, and why' is a concrete, repeatable move.

activities.title: Fraction-bar size argument: 1/3 > 1/5
feedback: Accept the chain only when it links the number of parts to the size of each part, not just 'the bar looks bigger'.
If the child believes a bigger denominator means a bigger piece, return to the shared bar split from the same whole and count/compare the actual pieces before re-stating the argument.
Treat 'it just is' as the start of a justification, not the end: ask 'convince a doubter'.
activities.rationale: Anchoring an argument in a shared representation lets a critique target the reasoning rather than the person, and directly addresses the common belief that a larger denominator names a bigger piece. For unit fractions the numerator is fixed at 1, so the comparison varies only the number of equal parts of the same whole. Concrete referents are age-appropriate for constructing arguments at this stage.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others; elementary students construct arguments using concrete referents; they distinguish correct logic from flawed, and if there is a flaw, explain what it is; all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions.
learnerActions: Using fraction bars or an area model showing the same whole split into 3 and into 5, state and justify which piece is bigger.
Build the chain: 'more equal parts means smaller pieces, so fifths are smaller than thirds, therefore 1/3 > 1/5.'
When a classmate claims '1/5 is bigger because 5 is bigger than 3', find and explain the flaw using the shared bar both of you can point at.
activities.intendedInsight: Splitting the same whole into MORE equal parts makes each part SMALLER, so a unit fraction with the larger denominator is the smaller number — and a representation both parties can point at keeps a critique about the reasoning, not the person.

activities.title: When is a check really a proof? Convince a doubter
feedback: Draw out that 'it works in one example' is evidence to explore, not a proof; ask what a doubter could still object to and what would be needed to be sure for every case.
For the inverse check, point out that 35 + 46 = 81, not 71 — so a careful exact check actually reveals 35 is wrong. 'Close to' only hints at plausibility; it does not prove the answer is right.
If the child treats one checked case as settling a general claim, offer a claim where a second case breaks it, and discuss what changed.
activities.rationale: Empirical/example-based reasoning predominates at this age and the shift to deductive justification is slow and fragile; explicitly surfacing that checking examples does not prove a general claim targets a documented developmental step. The 'close to' inverse-check prompt extends this to verifying a single computation and is an agent-added illustration, conservatively framed as a proposal rather than a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Empirical/example-based reasoning predominates in this age range and the transition to deductive justification is slow and fragile; recognising that checking examples does not prove a general claim is a key developmental step.

Reasoning develops along a describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder, and children's reasoning frequently runs ahead of their ability to communicate it, so a teacher must elicit and scribe the reasoning rather than judge it by fluency of telling.
learnerActions: Given a general claim and a single example that fits it, decide whether checking that one example proves the claim for all cases.
Explain why one confirming example is not a proof, and what would be needed to be convinced for every case.
Evaluate a weak check such as: 'A classmate says 71 − 46 = 35 is fine because 35 + 46 is close to 71. Is that a good way to check? What does it actually tell you?'
activities.intendedInsight: Evidence that falls short of a complete argument — a single confirming example, or an approximate 'close to' check — does not establish or verify a claim; distinguishing 'it works here / it's roughly right' from 'it must always work / it is exactly right' is a key step toward justification.

activities.title: Compare-and-annotate launch: sound vs flawed argument
feedback: After the reveal, ask the child to re-explain the flaw without the annotation open.
Move promptly from recognising the flaw to constructing or critiquing a new one, so the productive half is exercised.
activities.rationale: A static correct-vs-flawed pair with tap-to-reveal annotations can seed critique and model reasons, but it shows arguments rather than eliciting the child's own chain or responding to their reasoning; treat it as a launch for talk, not as the assessment. Tap-to-reveal is an optional interaction example, not a required mechanism.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others; elementary students construct arguments using concrete referents; they distinguish correct logic from flawed, and if there is a flaw, explain what it is; all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions.
learnerActions: Study a side-by-side pair of worked arguments for the same problem — one sound, one with a hidden error.
Tap each step to reveal the reason it does or does not follow, then say in your own words which argument holds and where the other breaks.
Use this only as a springboard: afterwards, construct your OWN correct chain or critique a fresh flawed example aloud.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing a correct and a flawed argument side by side can seed critique and vocabulary for 'why a step follows', but reading annotations is only a starting point for producing your own argument.

constraints: The productive half of this practice — constructing a multi-step argument and explaining a flaw in the child's own words — requires construction and talk; a scored fixed-answer format can test RECOGNISING a correct argument or spotting a flagged flawed step, but a 'spot the flawed step' multiple-choice item should be used only as a warm-up and its score should not be treated as evidence of the reasoning practice.

Static compare-and-annotate pairs are scaffolds: they can show and label arguments but cannot elicit the child's own chain or respond to their reasoning. Follow them immediately with construction or critique.

Error analysis is the practice: finding one clear faulty step and explaining it is the goal, not re-solving and comparing answers. Keep critique pointed at the shared representation so it targets the reasoning, not the person.
Scribe/revoice a child whose reasoning outruns their words; do not judge reasoning by fluency of telling or score it.

Distinguish an argument-skill gap from a prerequisite gap: if a child endorses 'always take the smaller from the larger', reteach the column-subtraction exchange concept with base-ten equipment before expecting critique of that algorithm.

This guidance is medium-flexible: a live partner, scribed classroom talk, paper worked examples, or a screen workspace can all carry it. Interaction examples (tile snapping, tapping a step, tap-to-reveal) are illustrative, not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the underlying teaching principle rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 71 − 46 = 25 (correct in the source). The flawed worked example's '35' is explicitly the peer's error to be critiqued, never presented as a valid answer. The exchange explanation (1 becomes 11, 11 − 6 = 5; tens become 6, 6 − 4 = 2, giving 25) is sound and preserved. Note also 35 + 46 = 81 ≠ 71, so the classmate's 'close to 71' inverse check would in fact expose the error; this is surfaced in the weak-evidence activity's feedback.

Self-audit of derived-fact chain: 6×8 = 60 − 12 = 48 is correct (6×10=60, 6×2=12). Note a wording inconsistency in the source: pedagogy and the first evidence item present the chain as 'since 6×10=60 and 6×2=12, then 6×8=60−12=48', but the third evidence item phrases it as 'since 6×8=48 and 6×2=12, then 6×10=60 so 6×8=60−12=48', which assumes the conclusion (6×8=48) as a premise — a circular/garbled ordering. Activities use the sound forward direction (6×10 and 6×2 ⇒ 6×8); the circular phrasing was not propagated.

Self-audit of fraction claim: 1/3 > 1/5 is correct and justified by more equal parts of the same whole meaning smaller pieces; both are unit fractions so only the number of parts varies. No 'denominator rule flips' language is used; same-whole scoping applies to comparing represented portions, while the fractions remain comparable as numbers.

The original labelled a conversation artefact 'ideal' and 3D 'poor/adds nothing'. Those are catalog fit rankings, not established pedagogical laws, and have been removed; the dialogic and workspace activities are presented as complementary options with stated affordances and limits rather than a universal 'only talk teaches this' claim.
Internal identifiers (microTopic and reteach-prerequisite IDs) were stripped from the guidance; the exchange prerequisite is retained conceptually only.

Activity 4 blends example-based generalisation (supported by Hoyles & Küchemann) with critique of an approximate single-computation 'close to' check; the 'close to' strand is an agent extension and is not directly supported by a cited source, though it is conservatively framed and its exact-check correction (35+46=81≠71) is mathematically sound.

probeDeeper: 'Show me the exact line where the thinking first goes wrong — put your finger on it.'
'Why can't you just swap it round and do 6 take away 1? What would you have to do instead?'
'A different classmate says 71 − 46 = 35 is fine because 35 + 46 is close to 71. Is that a good way to check? What does it actually tell you?'
'Now build me a correct chain for 71 − 46 out loud — start with what 71 really is.'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child locating the specific faulty STEP (flipping 1−6 into 6−1 instead of exchanging a ten) AND giving a reason grounded in place value (the 1 is part of 71, so you take a ten to make 11, then 11−6=5), rather than just announcing that 35 is the wrong answer.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges the peer's argument by answer-agreement, not by the reasoning: 'it's wrong because I got 25' — re-solves and compares totals without ever locating or explaining the faulty step.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redirect from answer to step: 'Don't tell me the right answer yet — show me the first line where their thinking stops being okay, and say why that line breaks.' Model once on a different flawed example.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child announces the correct answer or redoes the calculation but cannot point to WHICH step is wrong or WHY; treats 'different answer' as the whole critique.

errorPatterns.pattern: Accepts the smaller-from-larger step as fine — shares the bug: agrees you can 'just do 6 take 1' because 'you always take the little one from the big one.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: This is a genuine false belief about the algorithm — confront it with base-ten equipment: build 71, try to remove 6 ones, force the exchange. Reteach the exchange concept, not the argument skill.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child endorses the flipped subtraction, or hesitates only about the final total, treating column subtraction as digit-by-digit with the smaller digit always subtracted.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sees something is wrong and objects, but the objection stays at 'that's not right' — reasoning outruns communication, no because-clause emerges even though the child clearly senses the flaw.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT treat as not-knowing. Scribe/revoice: offer 'you can't do that because…?' and let the child complete it; point at base-ten blocks so the reason has something to attach to. The reasoning is present; only the telling lags.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Frowns, says 'no you can't do that' or 'it doesn't work like that' but cannot yet articulate the place-value reason when asked 'why not?'

responseLevels.gap: Only evaluates the answer ('it's 25, so they're wrong') or redoes the sum; cannot locate the faulty step or gives no reason.
responseLevels.full: Pinpoints the flipped-subtraction step AND explains the place-value reason it fails (the 1 stands for part of 71, so a ten must be exchanged to make 11−6=5), then reconstructs a correct because/therefore chain — and transfers the 'find the broken step and say why' move to a new flawed example unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Locates the wrong step (the digit-flip) but explains it as 'that's not the rule' or restates the correct procedure without the place-value reason; can describe the steps but not why the flawed one breaks.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is how a classmate worked out 71 − 46. They wrote: '1 take away 6 — I can't, so I'll do 6 take away 1, that's 5. Then 7 take away 4 is 3. So the answer is 35.' Is their thinking okay? Talk me through what they did, step by step, and tell me where — if anywhere — it goes wrong and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who genuinely constructs and critiques arguments identifies the exact broken step and explains the place-value reason it fails; a child who only checks answers will say 'it's wrong, it should be 25' (or redo the sum) without ever naming which step broke or why — same surface verdict, completely different reasoning. Because the error is a real, well-documented one (the 'always take smaller from larger' / smaller-from-larger bug), a child reasoning correctly and one reasoning by answer-agreement give observably different responses.
